o: Each processor runs exactly 4 tasks and finishes when its longest task finishes, so a processor available at time p assigned tasks T finishes at p + max(T). We minimize the maximum over processors. In example 1, giving the four biggest tasks (8,7,5,4) to the earliest processor (8) yields 16, and small tasks to the late processor yield 13.
k: Only the maximum task per processor matters, so each processor's load is start time plus its largest assigned task.
Exchange argument: pair the earliest-available processor with the globally largest tasks — swapping any assignment never decreases the maximum.

a.i: Sort processors ascending and tasks descending. Give processor i (earliest available) the block of 4 largest unassigned tasks. Any inversion (a later processor holding a bigger task than an earlier one) can be swapped without hurting the answer, proving optimality.
s: For each i, candidate = processorTime[i] + tasks[4*i].
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting both arrays dominates

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search on the Answer
a.i: Binary search the finish time T: greedily give each processor (in availability order) the largest remaining tasks that fit within T − p. Feasibility is monotone in T, so binary search converges. It is more code but generalizes when blocks aren't fixed-size.
s: Binary search T between max(pt)+min(task) and max(pt)+max(task).
Check feasibility: sort tasks descending, assign each processor up to 4 tasks with duration ≤ T − p.
a.t: O(n log n + n log V) — sorting plus binary search over the answer range
a.sp: O(n) — copies for sorting in some languages

w: Use the sorting greedy in interviews — it's short and provably optimal via an exchange argument. Pitfall: remember each processor takes exactly 4 tasks, so the pairing stride is 4. Follow-ups include variable core counts or tasks assignable in any quantity.
